fields.Front: Why introduce a cache in a system?
fields.Back: To reduce latency and load on the primary data store by serving frequently accessed data from faster storage.

fields.Front: In the cache-aside (lazy-loading) pattern, who is responsible for populating the cache on a miss?
fields.Back: The application: it reads from the cache, and on a miss it reads from the DB and writes the result into the cache itself.

fields.Front: In read-through caching, who populates the cache on a miss?
fields.Back: The cache itself — it sits in front of the DB and transparently loads missing data, so the application only ever talks to the cache.
Writes go to the cache and the underlying DB synchronously as one operation, keeping the cache always consistent with the DB but adding write latency.
Writes go to the cache immediately and are asynchronously flushed to the DB later, giving low write latency but risking data loss if the cache fails before flushing.

fields.Front: Cache-aside vs read-through: what's the key difference in responsibility?
fields.Back: In cache-aside the application manages loading the cache on a miss; in read-through the cache layer manages it transparently.

fields.Front: Why is TTL-based eviction useful even alongside LRU/LFU?
fields.Back: It guarantees data won't stay stale forever, bounding how out-of-date a cached value can get.

fields.Front: Why is cache invalidation considered a hard problem?
fields.Back: It's difficult to guarantee every cached copy of a piece of data is updated or removed exactly when the underlying data changes, especially across distributed caches and concurrent writes.
When a popular cached key expires or is evicted and many concurrent requests simultaneously miss the cache and hammer the backend to recompute the same value.
A cache stored in a single application instance's own memory — very fast, but not shared across instances and lost on restart.

fields.Front: What is a distributed cache, and give an example technology?
fields.Back: A cache shared across multiple application instances over the network, e.g. Redis or Memcached.

fields.Front: What is one key architectural difference between Redis and Memcached?
fields.Back: Redis supports rich data structures and persistence/replication; Memcached is a simpler, purely in-memory key-value cache.

fields.Front: What is the main tradeoff of a local cache vs a distributed cache?
fields.Back: Local caches are faster with no network hop but cause inconsistency across instances; distributed caches stay consistent across instances but add network latency.

fields.Front: What is a CDN's primary purpose?
fields.Back: To cache and serve content from servers geographically close to the user, reducing latency and offloading the origin server.
Storing copies of content at edge servers distributed near end users, rather than only at a central origin, so requests are served from the nearest location.
How closely the data in a cache matches the current true state of the underlying data source.

fields.Front: Name a core tradeoff in cache consistency design.
fields.Back: Stronger consistency (always fresh) typically costs more latency and invalidation overhead; weaker (eventual) consistency is faster but can serve stale data.
A request that finds the requested data already present in the cache.
A request for data not found in the cache, requiring a fetch from the slower underlying source.

fields.Text: The four common cache read/write patterns are {{c1::cache-aside}}, {{c2::read-through}}, {{c3::write-through}}, and {{c4::write-back}}.

Common cache eviction policies: {{c1::LRU}} (evicts the least recently used item), {{c2::LFU}} (evicts the least frequently used item), and {{c3::TTL}} (expires items after a fixed time regardless of usage).

Cache stampedes can be mitigated with techniques like {{c1::locking/mutex around the recompute}}, {{c2::early or probabilistic refresh before expiry}}, or {{c3::serving stale data while recomputing in the background}}.
